title: Attention, Meaning & Consolidation: Matching Technique to Purpose https://learningspy.co.uk/english-gcse/attention-meaning-consolidation-matching-teaching-to-purpose/
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau argues that teacher training built around discrete pedagogical techniques - cold calling, mini-whiteboards, visualisers - has a ceiling problem: he's repeatedly watched teachers execute a technique correctly and still deliver a lesson full of missed learning opportunities. Reflecting on Mary Kennedy's 2015 paper Parsing the Practice of Teaching and its five persistent problems of teaching, he lands on a simpler three-part lens borrowed from hearing Tom Sherrington speak at a conference: every lesson needs to secure attention, help students make meaning of new content, and give them a chance to consolidate it. Didau tests the framework live, teaching a staged lesson to a class of Year 10 students he'd never met, using cold calling, mini-whiteboards, and paired talk to build toward a single-sentence analytical answer about An Inspector Calls. He then has the audience retroactively sort his own technique choices into the attention/meaning/consolidation categories, demonstrating the framework as an analytic tool rather than just a design principle. The upshot is a reframing of instructional coaching: rather than assessing whether a teacher executed a named technique correctly, the more useful question is which of the three underlying purposes a given classroom moment is serving, and whether the chosen technique actually serves it.
points: Didau's opening diagnosis is that technique-only teacher training plateaus: he's watched teachers execute cold-calling or mini-whiteboards correctly and still produce lessons full of missed opportunities, suggesting technique fidelity isn't the same as instructional effectiveness.

He borrows Tom Sherrington's three-purpose lens - attention, making meaning, consolidation - as a simpler alternative to Mary Kennedy's five persistent problems of teaching, arguing it's more usable for evaluating which strategy to deploy and when.

His live demonstration lesson (an unfamiliar Year 10 class studying An Inspector Calls) turns the framework into an audit tool: after teaching, he had the audience sort his own techniques into the attention/meaning/consolidation categories.

The reframe's real value, in Didau's telling, is diagnostic: instead of asking did I use the right technique, teachers can ask which of the three purposes a moment in the lesson is actually serving, and pick a technique to match.
quotes: It's become increasingly clear to me that training teachers on how to use pedagogical techniques is of limited use. Over the past year or so I've lost count of the times I've watched a teacher act on feedback, improve how how they are, say, cold calling, or using a visualiser or mini-whiteboard, and yet still somehow the lesson is a series of missed opportunities

One of the points that stood out was the need to ensure that in every lesson students are paying attention, that they have opportunities to think about new content in a way which helps them make sense of it, and that they also need opportunities to consolidate what they have learned.

I explained the concepts of redundancy and concision as being hallmarks of academic language. I then asked them to think about whether there were any redundant words or phrases and how the answer could be made more concise.
Nothing particularly spectacular on my part, but I could see that the students all had a sense of having achieved something and they left the stage to hearty and well-deserved applause.

A few years ago I read (or at lest, skimmed) Mary Kennedy's 2015 paper, Parsing the Practice of Teaching and was struck, like so many others, by her analysis of five 'persistent problems' which all teachers have to solve every lesson.
